summary: Ages 11–13 (KS3; NGSS MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3): teach chemosynthesis by direct contrast with the already-known photosynthesis — both are producers fixing carbon from CO2 into food, but one is powered by light and the other by chemical energy (oxidising hydrogen sulphide, H2S, from vent fluid). Build a hydrothermal-vent food web where chemoautotrophic bacteria are the producers at the base, supporting tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs with no sunlight as the energy source. Then weigh the open, still-debated questions: could life have begun at vents, and why do agencies like NASA study vents as analogues for possible life on icy ocean worlds such as Europa and Enceladus? Key targets include correcting 'all producers are green plants / all food chains start with sunlight', distinguishing chemical energy from the vent's heat, and distinguishing an energy source from a food source.
misconceptions: 'All producers photosynthesise / all food chains start with sunlight' — the key misconception chemosynthesis overturns.
'The vent's HEAT is the energy source for the food web' — conflating heat with the chemical energy bacteria actually oxidise.
'Producers must be plants/green' — not recognising bacteria as producers.
'Chemosynthesis is just photosynthesis in the dark' — missing that the energy source is fundamentally chemical, not light.
Treating origin-of-life/alien-ocean claims as proven rather than as reasoned, evidence-based hypotheses.

activities.title: Build a vent food web on a different power source
steps: First build (or label) a familiar sunlit web: Sun → phytoplankton/plants → consumers, and mark where the energy enters.
Now build a hydrothermal-vent food web set in permanent darkness. Try to place the Sun at the base and notice it cannot power this web — no sunlight reaches kilometres down.

Choose the base's actual energy source from options including 'sunlight', 'the vent's heat', and 'chemical energy (oxidising hydrogen sulphide, H2S)'. Select the chemical-energy option so chemoautotrophic bacteria become the producers.
Extend the web: bacteria → tube worms / giant clams → vent crabs, and trace the energy flow from the chemical source upward.
Set the two webs side by side and fill a comparison table: inputs, energy source, and product (food/organic matter from CO2) for photosynthesis vs chemosynthesis.
activities.insight: Photosynthesis is not the only way to build a food web. Producers do the same job — making food by fixing carbon from CO2 — but can be powered either by light (photosynthesis) or by chemical energy from oxidising H2S (chemosynthesis). Bacteria, not green plants, are the producers at a vent, and the community's energy source is chemical, not the Sun.

activities.title: Reason with an astrobiologist: did life begin at vents, and where else might it be?
steps: Take on the question in role: ask and answer 'Why look at hydrothermal vents to search for life beyond Earth?' and 'Could life have begun at vents?'

Set out the reasoning: if life needs chemical energy, water and minerals — which vents supply without sunlight as the energy source — then sunless environments elsewhere are not automatically lifeless.
Apply the analogy to Europa and Enceladus: these icy moons may have subsurface oceans and hydrothermal chemistry but no sunlight; discuss what makes them candidates and what remains unknown.
State explicitly which parts are established (vent communities exist and run without sunlight as their energy source) and which are open hypotheses (origin of life at vents; life on ocean moons).
Weigh at least one piece of evidence for and one source of uncertainty before giving a tentative, reasoned position.
activities.insight: Vents reshape the search for life because they show a food web can run on chemical energy and water rather than light. Whether life began at vents, and whether ocean moons host life, are genuine open scientific questions to be argued from evidence and uncertainty — not settled facts.

activities.title: Explore and interrogate a vent cross-section
steps: Explore a labelled vent scene: mineral-rich fluid rising, bacterial mats, tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs — tracing which organism depends on which.
Open a photosynthesis/chemosynthesis comparison showing inputs, energy source and product aligned for each.
Examine an Earth-vent ↔ Europa/Enceladus analogue panel and state what the two settings share.
Answer short checks: name the producer at a vent; name its energy source (oxidising H2S) and its carbon source (CO2); and explain why the community survives with no sunlight as its energy source.
activities.insight: A vent community is a complete food web whose base producers are bacteria powered by chemical energy, with no sunlight as the energy source; the same comparison that defines photosynthesis clarifies how chemosynthesis differs.

activities.title: Check and discriminate the concept
steps: Answer a two-tier diagnostic: given giant tube worms and clams thriving around bacteria in permanent darkness, decide whether sunlight is the energy source the producers capture — and if not, state what is and how the bacteria capture it.

Give the full answer: chemoautotrophic bacteria oxidise H2S (using oxygen dissolved in seawater) for energy and use it to build food from CO2; tube worms, clams and crabs depend on those bacteria; the energy the producers capture is chemical energy from vent fluid (from reactions in the Earth's crust), not sunlight.
Compare a leaf and a vent bacterium: what is the same (both build food from CO2) and what differs (light energy vs chemical energy)?
Predict: if a vent stopped emitting hydrogen sulphide, what happens to the tube worms, and why?
Contrast the two energy sources, identify the vent producer, and reason about how far the Europa/Enceladus analogue holds and what remains unknown.
activities.insight: Secure understanding means naming chemosynthesis, identifying the oxidised chemical (H2S) as the energy source, keeping CO2 as the carbon source, and transferring the idea to origin-of-life and ocean-world reasoning — not merely using the word 'chemosynthesis' as a label.

checkQuestion: At a hydrothermal vent, kilometres down in permanent darkness, giant tube worms and clams flourish around bacteria — with no sunlight ever reaching them. A student says 'the energy must still trace back to the Sun somehow, because photosynthesis is where all food energy on Earth begins'. Is the Sun the ultimate energy source for a vent community? If not, what is, and how do the bacteria capture it?
checkAnswer: No — vent communities are independent of sunlight. Their base is CHEMOSYNTHESIS, not photosynthesis: chemoautotrophic bacteria get energy by oxidising chemicals (especially hydrogen sulphide, H2S) streaming from the vent, and use that energy to build food (organic matter) from CO2. Tube worms, clams and vent crabs then depend on those bacteria. So the ultimate energy source is chemical energy from the Earth's interior, not the Sun. This is why vents matter for ideas about the origin of life and why agencies like NASA study them as analogues for possible life on ocean worlds such as Europa and Enceladus, where there is no sunlight but there may be hydrothermal chemistry.
